Victor Frankenstein ask why
people have to die. Early death was a
common phenomenon at the time that
Mary Shelley wrote her novel (1816-1818).
There were several tragedies within her
own personal experience. Her mother

died only a few days after she was born.
At the age of 16 she ran away with the
poet Percy Shelley to France, an later
Switzerland and Italy. Together they
had several children but all of them,
except for one son, died in childhood.
Their friend, the poet John Keats, died
in Rome at the age of 26. The following
year Shelley himself was drowned in
Italy at the age of 30.

l been some
important developments
in medicine by the early
19th century. The study
of anatomy, in particular,
carried out through the
dissection of human
bodies, was quite advanced.
In the novel Victor Frankenstein studies human anatomy before
attempting to construct his creature.

However, by modern standards, medicine was still very primitive
in this period. Doctors did not know very much about bacteria.
Vaccination had only recently been discovered and was not
common. There were no antibiotics. Infectious diseases spread
rapidly and killed many people, especially in the crowded cities,
where sanitation was very poor. Surgeons carried out operations
wearing their street clothes, with no anaesthetics and no
sterilisation of equipment.
Half of their patients
died from infections
caused by the operations
themselves.

Giving birth to a child
was another dangerous
experience, for both
mothers and babies.
Families were large
but children were
particularly vulnerable
to disease and many
did not survive

childhood.

} electrical energy was still a

Scientists were only starting to

In America in 1752,
Benjamin Franklin perfor-

He proved that lightning is
electricity. In the following

Galvani (1737-1798) became famous

He discovered that electrical

For Europeans the early 19th century was still the age of explora-

enormous areas of the globe were still unexplored, including
Australia and the Pacific Ocean, the interior of Africa, large parts of
North and South America and the polar regions. Nobody knew
what strange things were still waiting to be discovered.

cientific expeditions travelled to all parts of the world
during this period. Their purpose was to expand geographical
knowledge and to study the plants and animals they found.

James Cook, a captain in the British Navy, carried out expedi-
